knowledge_graph.title: Monoclonal antibody
knowledge_graph.description: A monoclonal antibody is an antibody produced from a cell lineage made by cloning a unique white blood cell. All subsequent antibodies derived this way trace back to a unique parent cell. Monoclonal antibodies are identical and can thus have monovalent affinity, binding only to a particular epitope.

related_questions.question: How does a monoclonal antibody treatment work?
related_questions.snippet: Some monoclonal antibodies can trigger an immune system response that can destroy the outer wall (membrane) of a cancer cell. Blocking cell growth. Some monoclonal antibodies block the connection between a cancer cell and proteins that promote cell growth — an activity that is necessary for cancer growth and survival.

related_questions.question: What is a disadvantage of using monoclonal antibodies as treatment?
related_questions.snippet: Monoclonal antibody therapy has several limitations, including limited availability and accessibility, high cost, the need for early intervention, potential resistance and mutation, and the risk of side effects. text_blocks.snippet: Monoclonal antibody treatment involves using laboratory-produced antibodies to target and neutralize specific molecules or cells in the body, aiding in the fight against diseases like cancer and infections. These engineered antibodies are designed to mimic the body's natural immune response, helping to either block harmful pathogens from entering cells or mark them for destruction by the immune system.
snippet_highlighted_words: using laboratory-produced antibodies to target and neutralize specific molecules or cells in the body, aiding in the fight against diseases like cancer and infections

list.snippet: Monoclonal antibodies are proteins created in a lab that are designed to bind to a specific target, such as a protein on a cancer cell or a virus.
They are "monoclonal" because they are all identical copies of a single antibody, ensuring they target the same specific molecule.
This targeted approach allows for a more precise and potentially more effective treatment compared to traditional therapies.

list.title: For infections (like COVID-19):
list.snippet: mAbs can be designed to bind to the spike protein on viruses like SARS-CoV-2, preventing the virus from entering and infecting healthy cells.

list.title: For cancer:
list.snippet: mAbs can target antigens on cancer cells, either directly killing them or flagging them for destruction by the body's immune system. They can also carry drugs or toxins directly to cancer cells.

list.title: For other diseases:
list.snippet: mAbs are also used to treat autoimmune diseases (like rheumatoid arthritis), prevent blood clots, and treat organ transplant rejection.

list.title: Cancer treatment:
list.snippet: Many mAbs are used to treat different types of cancer, either alone or in combination with other treatments.

list.title: Infectious disease treatment:
list.snippet: mAbs have been used to treat COVID-19 and other viral infections.

list.title: Autoimmune disease treatment:
list.snippet: mAbs can help regulate the immune system in conditions like rheumatoid arthritis.

list.title: Other applications:
list.snippet: mAbs are also used in treating blood clots and preventing organ transplant rejection.
Monoclonal antibody treatments are typically administered intravenously (through a vein).
Side effects can occur, including allergic reactions, fever, chills, and other symptoms.
While effective, monoclonal antibody therapy is not a replacement for vaccination in the case of infectious diseases.
